problem_plain: Modern AI models spend most of their time waiting for data to travel from memory chips to the processor, not actually doing math. When a model generates a single word, it must haul tens of gigabytes of stored numbers — its learned weights and the model's running notes — across a wire that can only move a fraction of that data per second. The processor sits idle most of the time, starved for numbers to work on.
why_plain: The chips that do math have gotten dramatically faster over decades, but the wires connecting chips to memory have not kept pace — moving a byte still takes roughly the same time it did years ago. This gap between math speed and data-movement speed is called the memory wall, and AI workloads hit it especially hard because they read enormous tables of learned numbers and the model's running notes in patterns that defeat simple tricks for keeping data nearby.
approach_plain: The papers in this theme attack the memory wall from three directions: bringing the math closer to where data already lives (doing math inside the memory), smarter decisions about which data lives where and for how long (tiering, fetching data early, compressing, and smarter eviction), and restructuring how programs hand data between storage layers (computing near or inside the storage drive, using a fast link to extra memory, and tuning hardware and software together). Together they aim to cut the number of bytes that must cross any wire before useful work happens.

groups.heading: Running math inside or right next to memory chips
groups.explain: Instead of shipping data from memory to a processor, these designs place small math units inside or immediately beside the memory chip itself. A memory chip's internal wiring carries far more data per second than any external wire, so doing even simple math there — multiplying rows of numbers by a single column, computing distances, adding things up — can eliminate most of the costly external data movement. This is what 'doing math inside the memory' means.

papers.name: CENT
papers.gloss: Runs the model without a GPU, using 32 memory modules that have math units built into their memory chips; delivers 2.3x more answers per second and costs 5.2x less per answer than four top data-center GPUs.

papers.name: PAPI
papers.gloss: Mixes doing-math-inside-the-memory units with GPU-like chips; a live monitor watches each step of the model's word-generation and routes it to whichever chip best matches whether that step is math-heavy or data-movement-heavy.

Runs privacy-preserving encrypted math (where you compute on locked data without unlocking it) on doing-math-inside-the-memory hardware, by keeping numbers that are used together physically close; 4 to 209 times faster than earlier accelerators.

papers.name: PUSHtap
papers.gloss: Arranges database rows so both the main CPU and the in-memory math units can read the same copy of data without converting its format; delivers 3.4x faster analytics queries and 4.4x faster transaction queries from one shared copy.

papers.name: AsyncDIMM
papers.gloss: Lets the host chip and the math unit on a standard memory module work at the same time instead of taking turns; 1.19 to 1.92 times faster than designs where they must wait for each other.

papers.name: PROCA
papers.gloss: Runs a statistical sampling method (repeatedly drawing random guesses and accepting or rejecting them) inside memory chips; predicts early whether a guess will be accepted before finishing all the math; 172 to 4,871 times faster than a standard CPU.

papers.name: PAISE
papers.gloss: Moves the model's attention step — where each new word checks against the model's running notes — from the GPU to memory chips that have math units built in; rearranges data so many memory banks work in parallel; cuts attention time by up to 48%.

papers.name: FACIL
papers.gloss: Changes how memory addresses are mapped so the model's learned weights can be read simultaneously by both the in-memory math unit and the main chip, without copying data twice; cuts the time until the first word appears by 2.4 to 2.6 times.

papers.name: Piccolo
papers.gloss: Places only a lightweight traffic-routing function — not full math — inside memory chips, keeping cost low while avoiding the waste of reading large chunks of memory just to use a few bytes; up to 3.28 times faster and 59.7% less energy for graph data.

papers.name: UniNDP
papers.gloss: A shared set of software tools that writes programs for many different doing-math-inside-the-memory chip designs using one common language; improves how well programs are mapped to hardware by 1.05 to 3.43 times over tools written per chip.

papers.name: GoPIM
papers.gloss: Runs graph-learning networks on memory chips that store values as electrical resistance levels; a learned planner allocates hardware resources across the network's pipeline stages; up to 191 times faster and 16 times more energy-efficient than prior designs.

papers.name: EOD
papers.gloss: A math unit beside the memory chip combines compressed graph data without first sending it to the main chip to decompress; 981 times faster on the combining step and 18 times faster end-to-end compared to doing it on a GPU.

papers.name: NMP-PaK
papers.gloss: Places pipelined math units inside memory module buffer chips to assemble genome graphs from DNA fragments; actual memory bandwidth used rises from 6.5% to 44%, giving 16 times CPU speed and 5.7 times GPU speed.

papers.name: ANSMET
papers.gloss: Math units beside memory chips compute rough lower-bound distances as data streams out and stop reading early when a candidate is clearly too far away; about 8 times total speedup for searching a database for the closest matching entry.

papers.name: HeterRAG
papers.gloss: Pairs cheap high-capacity memory-module math units (for messy lookup steps) with high-speed memory math units (for the model's dense number-crunching steps) in one system that retrieves documents and then generates answers.

papers.name: OptiPIM
papers.gloss: Frames the problem of mapping a neural network onto a doing-math-inside-the-memory chip as a math optimization problem and solves it automatically in under four minutes; at least 1.9 times better than hand-tuned guesses.

papers.name: DReX
papers.gloss: Logic inside the memory chip filters out far-away entries before they leave the chip; a math unit beside memory then does an exact close-match search on what remains; 6 to 7 times faster first-word output with no loss in accuracy.

papers.name: ATiM
papers.gloss: A compiler that automatically finds the best way to split and schedule math for a real commercial memory chip that has processors built in (UPMEM), without hand-coding; up to 8.2 times faster on model layers compared to manual approaches.

papers.name: DX100
papers.gloss: Reorders up to 16,384 indirect memory lookups — patterns like 'read position B[i], then go fetch A at that position' — before sending requests to memory chips, giving 500 times more look-ahead than a memory controller normally has; 2.6 times faster than four CPU cores.

papers.name: Stratum
papers.gloss: Stacks doing-math-inside-the-memory processors above a tall memory chip bonded at tiny scale; a lightweight classifier predicts which specialist weights will be needed next and moves them to faster internal tiers; 8.3 times faster word generation over a GPU baseline.

papers.name: Pimba
papers.gloss: Two memory banks share one math unit by interleaving reads from one with writes from the other, cutting chip area in half; handles both recurrent model state updates and the model's attention step; 4.1 times more words per second than a GPU.

papers.name: ORCHES
papers.gloss: The GPU handles the model's initial read of a prompt while doing-math-inside-the-memory units handle word-by-word generation; overlapping these steps speculatively during multi-step reasoning gives 4.2 times speedup over GPU-only.

papers.name: FALA
papers.gloss: Routes data that will be reused through the CPU's fast on-chip memory and data that will only be touched once through in-memory math units; reads only the specific graph data needed rather than a full memory row; 1.56 times faster, 35% less energy.

papers.name: Ecco
papers.gloss: A compress-and-expand unit sits between the GPU's fast on-chip memory and the memory chips; compresses the model's weights and running notes 4 times using a compact encoding scheme; 64 parallel expanders match the on-chip memory's speed; 2.9 times faster with no accuracy loss.

papers.name: REIS
papers.gloss: Math running inside a solid-state storage drive's own controller searches for the closest matching entries and fetches the relevant documents together, removing the usual round-trip to the main chip for a retrieval-then-generate system.

An adaptable math unit inside a storage drive converts a text query into a vector of numbers and searches for close matches entirely inside the drive; 4.3 times faster than CPU plus drive, 1.5 times faster than GPU plus memory chip for document retrieval.

papers.name: CrossBit
papers.gloss: Adds wires inside flash memory chips so simple bit operations can span across multiple columns of storage cells; enables error correction and database filtering inside the flash chip itself; 2.1 times faster and 2.5 times more energy-efficient than prior in-flash designs.

papers.name: Folded Banks (FB-HBM)
papers.gloss: Redistributes memory sub-banks across layers of a tall stacked memory chip using short vertical connections, turning long slow horizontal wires into short fast vertical ones; improves fine-grained random-access bandwidth without adding external math logic.

papers.name: MagiCache
papers.gloss: Each row of fast on-chip memory can be switched dynamically between acting as a data store and acting as a math lane; chaining instructions hides wait time by computing on data as it arrives; 1.19 to 1.61 times over prior do-math-in-cache designs.

papers.name: MVE
papers.gloss: A new set of math instructions describes up to four-dimensional access patterns, letting a mobile phone's math unit built from its own fast on-chip memory use 60% of its compute lanes instead of only 23%; 2.9 times faster than standard mobile math instructions at 8.8 times lower energy.

papers.name: ASDR
papers.gloss: Maps 3D scene reconstruction (a method that builds photorealistic 3D views from many photos) onto doing-math-inside-the-memory chips; fewer samples are taken per camera ray and nearby rays share data to avoid repeated reads from the chip.

papers.name: CMSwitch
papers.gloss: The first compiler that notices when a doing-math-inside-the-memory chip can flip its arrays between math mode and storage mode; uses a math solver to decide per layer which mode to use; 1.31 times average speedup over always picking one mode.

papers.name: ER-DCIM
papers.gloss: A doing-math-inside-the-memory chip that corrects its own math errors in real time when running at low voltage; catches errors in the add-and-multiply operations themselves using a compact checking code, not just at the memory cell level.

papers.name: HyFlexPIM
papers.gloss: A resistance-based memory chip that mixes analog and digital math; fine-tuning concentrates the model's most important weights into 5 to 10% of cells (kept in reliable single-bit mode), letting 90 to 95% use efficient two-bit cells with under 1% accuracy loss; 1.86 times more throughput.

The first real-hardware test of a commercial doing-math-inside-the-memory chip with 2 million 1-bit processors under a retrieve-then-generate workload; three data-arrangement improvements yield 54 to 118 times lower energy use than a GPU.

groups.heading: Using a fast link to extra memory: giving a server more memory through a high-speed cable
groups.explain: A fast link to extra memory (CXL — Compute Express Link) is a new electrical standard that lets a server treat extra memory modules, storage drives, or even other compute boards as if they were directly attached RAM, plugged into the same slot a graphics card uses. This expands how much memory a server can see without redesigning its processor chip. The catch is that this extra memory arrives 140 to 410 billionths of a second later than memory on the main board, so systems must be smart about what lives in fast memory versus slow memory and when to move data between them.

papers.name: Melody
papers.gloss: Runs 265 different programs across four real fast-link-to-extra-memory devices and five chip platforms to measure exactly where delays come from; breaks each memory access into sub-steps so engineers can see which specific step is the bottleneck.

papers.name: HybridTier
papers.gloss: Tracks both how often a page has been read over its lifetime and whether it has been read recently, using compact counting structures; uses both signals to decide whether each page should live in fast local memory or slower extra memory; up to 91% faster than earlier tiering systems.

papers.name: M5
papers.gloss: Places hardware counters for how often each memory page — and even individual 64-byte chunks within a page — is read directly inside the fast-link controller chip; tracks accesses at fine grain and moves only the hot bytes, not the full page; 14% faster than letting the CPU manage migrations.

papers.name: CTXNL
papers.gloss: Gives database code the ability to turn off full consistency-checking overhead for data that does not need it, item by item; avoids the cost of keeping every read perfectly synchronized across chips for loosely shared data; 2.1 times the throughput of standard fast-link memory sharing.

papers.name: ByteFS
papers.gloss: A file system that sends small random reads through the byte-by-byte fast-link path and large sequential writes through the block-at-a-time path of a storage drive that supports both modes, using each path for what it does best.

papers.name: SkyByte
papers.gloss: Bridges the mismatch between the fast-link's byte-by-byte reads and flash storage's page-at-a-time writes using a small write buffer inside the drive's own controller; the operating system switches to other work during long flash waits; 6 times faster than a plain fast-link storage drive.

papers.name: LIA
papers.gloss: Runs the model on one GPU but offloads large math steps to CPUs that have built-in matrix-multiply instructions, and uses a fast link to extra memory to hold more of the model than fits in GPU memory alone; up to 19 times lower delay than offloading to GPU memory only.

papers.name: CXLfork
papers.gloss: Uses fast-link shared memory to copy a running program onto a remote server without serializing or moving its entire state; cuts local memory use by 87% and starts new server instances 2.26 times faster for short-lived cloud tasks.

papers.name: ArtMem
papers.gloss: A learning agent decides when to move memory pages between fast chips and slower extra memory, and learns to stop migrating at all when the fast tier has free space; 35 to 172% faster than fixed placement rules.

papers.name: UGPU
papers.gloss: Dynamically carves a single GPU into unequal sections with different amounts of math and memory; uses the short vertical wires inside a tall stacked memory chip to move pages between memory layers in parallel rather than one at a time, reducing the cost of reconfiguration.

groups.heading: Fetching data early: getting data before the processor asks for it
groups.explain: Fetching data early means a hardware or software unit predicts what data will be needed soon and retrieves it from main memory in advance, hiding the wait time behind ongoing math. These papers design smarter early-fetch systems that handle irregular patterns — following pointers through a graph, doing indirect lookups like 'go to position B[i] and read A there' — that defeat simple approaches which only work when data is read in a straight line.

papers.name: Gaze
papers.gloss: A hardware unit that fetches data early by learning the spatial pattern of which memory addresses are read together within a region, rather than just looking at the instruction that triggered the read; 5.7 to 11.4% more instructions completed per second over prior spatial fetchers.

papers.name: Alecto
papers.gloss: For each memory request, automatically picks the best early-fetch strategy from several competing approaches based on that request's access type; cuts the energy used to store tracking information by 48% while covering more cases accurately.

papers.name: MOKA/DRIPPER
papers.gloss: Decides on each early fetch whether reaching across a memory page boundary is worth the overhead; uses a small learned predictor sensitive to how busy the address-lookup hardware is; 1.7 to 3.3% faster than always crossing or never crossing.

papers.name: RecMG
papers.gloss: Separate learned models guide what to keep in fast memory and what to fetch early for the large lookup tables used in recommendation systems, across a two-level memory setup of chips and drives; 43% faster end-to-end recommendation answers.

papers.name: Magellan
papers.gloss: A compiler-based early-fetch system that maps out data dependencies across nested loops to handle multi-level indirect lookups in graph and math workloads; 1.14 times average speedup with 25% fewer times the processor has to wait for data.

papers.name: Prophet
papers.gloss: Uses recorded run information to add hints into a program's binary that help existing hardware early-fetch engines manage their on-chip bookkeeping storage better; 14% faster than the previous best early-fetch approach.

papers.name: IPEX
papers.gloss: An add-on layer for early-fetch hardware on devices powered by harvested energy (like radio waves); suppresses fetches that will be lost when the device loses power based on predicting when the next outage will happen; saves 7.9% energy on average.

papers.name: MAMA
papers.gloss: Each CPU core runs its own policy for how aggressively to fetch data early, but a central supervisor tracks total bandwidth used across all cores to stop them collectively flooding the memory wire; 2.1% more overall work done, 10% fairer between cores.

papers.name: TSP+MRS
papers.gloss: In systems that run many tiny tasks (each about 100 steps long — too short for normal early-fetch to help), starts fetching a task's data the moment the task enters the queue; a scheduler then holds the task back until its data has arrived; up to 3.1 times faster.

papers.name: Hierarchical Prefetching
papers.gloss: Groups hundreds of kilobytes of related program code into named bundles using static analysis of the program file, then fetches an entire bundle when any entry point in it is detected; stays useful even when code branches in unexpected directions; 6.6% gain over the prior best code-fetch approach.

papers.name: Skia
papers.gloss: Keeps a lightweight record of recently evicted branch targets so the instruction-fetch unit can keep predicting correct addresses even after the main branch-target table runs out of room.
A joint management policy for the instruction address-lookup table and the instruction cache that stops them from independently evicting the same code regions and then both having to re-fetch them.

papers.name: EDBP
papers.gloss: A predictor for energy-harvesting devices that identifies which fast on-chip memory slots will not be read again before the next power outage, then powers those slots off early; saves 9.8% total energy.

papers.name: SoMa
papers.gloss: A compiler tool that plans when to fetch tensors from memory chips across several fused neural network layers at once rather than one layer at a time; 2.1 times faster and 37% less energy than prior approaches that fuse layers without planning data movement.

papers.name: NUPEA
papers.gloss: On chips where many small math units are spread across a grid, places the instructions that load data on the math units physically nearest to where that data lives; 28% faster than placing load instructions uniformly across the grid.

papers.name: CHESS/SBP
papers.gloss: A branch predictor for cloud services that records the decision-by-decision path of previous requests and replays those paths for new requests that follow similar code routes; reaches within 5% of a fully warmed-up predictor from a cold start, using only 18 kilobytes of extra storage.

papers.name: Phelps
papers.gloss: Runs all hard-to-predict branches in a helper thread that checks every possibility unconditionally each loop; feeds results to the main thread in step-by-step order so the main thread never stalls on a wrong prediction.

Shows that simple in-order chips (which run instructions one at a time, never reordering them) can use bold value guessing without needing recovery logic, because order is always known; recovers 86% of the speed advantage that out-of-order chips get, with 38% more instructions per clock.

Starts predicting branches several steps early by noticing that only one or two of all possible combinations of intermediate branch outcomes actually happen at runtime; cuts the energy overhead of early branch prediction from 14.6 times normal to 1.5 times, with a 4.4% speed gain.

papers.name: DeepContext
papers.gloss: A lightweight layer that links Python code calls to the actual GPU operations they trigger across the full AI software stack, making it easy to see which step is the real bottleneck; guided optimization based on its findings yields 1.06 to 1.66 times speedup.

groups.heading: Deciding what to keep and what to throw out of fast on-chip memory
groups.explain: Fast on-chip memory holds only a small amount of data. When it fills up and new data arrives, something must be thrown out. Choosing badly means the processor has to re-fetch that data from slow memory chips very soon. These papers design smarter eviction rules — often by watching past access patterns, using hints from the compiler that wrote the program, or managing both instruction and data streams together in chips with many cores.

papers.name: Garibaldi
papers.gloss: Tracks which instruction caused each piece of data to be loaded; if throwing out an instruction's slot would also lose data that instruction will need again soon, the policy protects it; 13.2% average speedup and 10% less energy on a 40-core server.

papers.name: TRRIP
papers.gloss: The compiler labels each block of code as hot, warm, or cold; the operating system passes this label through existing page-table bits to the hardware; fast on-chip memory keeps hot instruction blocks at highest priority; 3.9% speedup and 27% fewer instruction misses on mobile.

papers.name: IBM Telum Cache
papers.gloss: IBM's Telum II chip spreads its fast on-chip memory across stacked chips joined together, with an adaptive rule for how long data persists; keeps over 90% of its processors busy while running both business transaction and generative AI workloads at the same time.

papers.name: PACIPV
papers.gloss: Tries every combination of rules for when to insert and when to promote data in fast on-chip memory to find the best policy for code-heavy server workloads; matches complex learned policies with almost no extra hardware cost.

papers.name: FLACK/FURBYS
papers.gloss: Derives a new theoretical best-possible eviction rule for the decoded-instruction cache (where instructions are stored after being translated into simpler steps) that beats the classical optimal algorithm; a practical version using recorded run data cuts misses 14% over the standard least-recently-used rule and improves performance per watt 3.1%.

papers.name: Drishti
papers.gloss: Trains a reuse predictor on accesses from each core across all fast-memory slices, but keeps training samples local per slice to avoid flooding the wiring between chips; nearly doubles the benefit of prior smart eviction approaches on 32-core systems.

papers.name: Avalanche
papers.gloss: A math chip for multiplying matrices with mostly-zero entries (skipping unimportant numbers) reorders one matrix's columns so related data lands in the same fast-memory slot, then evicts fully finished intermediate results early to free space; 1.97 times over prior similar chips on a 6.15 square-millimeter design.

papers.name: Gemina
papers.gloss: Coordinates two memory-saving techniques — merging identical memory pages into one copy, and grouping small pages into large ones to speed up address lookups — so using both together preserves 96% of the memory savings while recovering 43% of the lookup-speed loss that merging alone causes.

papers.name: OASIS
papers.gloss: Detects which data objects in a many-GPU system have stable versus shifting access patterns, and assigns different move-or-copy policies per object and per phase without needing the programmer to annotate anything; 64% faster than standard on-first-touch placement.

papers.name: Necro-reaper
papers.gloss: New processor instructions let the compiler and memory manager tell hardware to skip loading or saving data that has already been freed by the program; cuts data movement 26% and raises throughput 6% in large-scale server workloads.

papers.name: TDRAM
papers.gloss: Adds tiny comparison circuits directly inside a tall stacked memory chip so the memory chip itself checks whether a requested address is stored there, and only sends data back to the CPU when it is; 1.23 times faster and 21% less energy.

papers.name: MPW
papers.gloss: Groups pending GPU address-translation requests that share the same page-table structure and sends multiple lookups in parallel from one translation unit; cuts the time requests spend waiting in queue by 87% and improves GPU throughput by 56%.

papers.name: Heliostat
papers.gloss: Reuses the address-lookup traversal hardware already built into GPUs for 3D rendering (which walks tree structures to find which triangle a ray hits) as extra address-translation engines, since both tasks walk the same kind of tree; 1.93 times faster at 1.5% the chip area of dedicated units.

papers.name: NACHO
papers.gloss: Builds write-after-read dependency detection directly into the fast on-chip memory controller for energy-harvesting devices, removing a separate tracking module and cutting how often the device must save its state; 54% less overhead at runtime and 82% fewer writes to the persistent memory.

papers.name: WarmCache
papers.gloss: Uses a type of memory (magnetic-resistive) with intentionally relaxed hold time so fast on-chip memory survives typical short power outages; a compiler-driven check corrects any bits that drifted during the outage on restart; 1.3 to 1.4 times faster than prior energy-harvesting fast-memory designs.

papers.name: Pivot
papers.gloss: Prioritizes only the specific memory requests from important co-located tasks that are actively blocking the processor pipeline — not all requests from those tasks — at every level of the memory chain; up to 2.76 times more work done by background tasks as a result.

papers.name: IRIS
papers.gloss: A mobile camera's image chip reuses edge-detection and motion maps it already computed for noise reduction to score how important each image region is; low-importance regions are shrunk before saving to memory, cutting bandwidth by 55% with under 1% quality loss.

groups.heading: Managing the model's running notes for fast AI serving
groups.explain: Large language models keep a record of the conversation so far — the model's running notes — that grows with every new word and can fill the GPU's memory entirely. These papers focus on moving, compressing, or scheduling these running notes so they do not become the bottleneck when many users are asking questions at the same time.

papers.name: Aqua
papers.gloss: When a request is paused mid-answer, moves the model's running notes across the fast chip-to-chip wire inside the same server to a neighboring GPU rather than to slow CPU memory; 4 times more answers per second and 20 times faster responses over prior AI serving systems.

papers.name: NEO
papers.gloss: Sets the CPU reading the model's running notes against the model's stored weights at the same time on the GPU; the transfer of data between CPU and GPU happens behind the scenes while both sides are working; up to 7.5 times more throughput on consumer GPUs.

papers.name: FPDT
papers.gloss: Trains models on text sequences up to 2 million words long by streaming chunks through a double buffer — the GPU processes one chunk while the next is already traveling across the chip-to-chip wire; handles 16 times longer sequences than prior work on the same hardware.

papers.name: LLM.265
papers.gloss: Reuses the GPU's built-in video encoding and decoding hardware (the same chips used for streaming video) as a compressor for all the model's number types — learned weights, intermediate values, training updates, and running notes — without adding new silicon.

papers.name: GSArch
papers.gloss: Labels 3D scene data units (small cloud-like dots used in a new photorealistic rendering method) as hot (used by many pixels) or cold; caches hot ones in fast on-chip memory to avoid re-reading them from memory chips during training; up to 6.5 times faster than a top data-center GPU.

Shows that searching for an exact match in a document database can be faster end-to-end than an approximate search, because it finds fewer but more relevant documents, giving the model less to read; this motivates building hardware that does exact search efficiently.

groups.heading: Computing near or inside the storage drive: filtering data before it leaves the drive
groups.explain: Storage drives hold far more data than any memory chip, but reading data from a drive and sending it to the processor wastes bandwidth on items that will be thrown away immediately. These papers push simple computation — filtering rows, matching names, compressing, finding close matches — into the storage device itself so only the relevant fraction of data ever travels across the wire.

papers.name: UPP
papers.gloss: Defines a compact set of instructions for database filter rules; the database compiles any SQL filter into those instructions and sends them to a flash-based smart drive where they run on stored data directly; 1.2 to 7.9 times faster query answers.

papers.name: ANVIL
papers.gloss: Matches name keys inside the flash chips of a standard solid-state drive for key-value store lookups; only matching entries leave the drive; 4 to 25 times faster than a conventional solid-state drive depending on the workload.

papers.name: Fusion
papers.gloss: An object store for analysis that lays out files so filter rules can be checked at the storage nodes before sending data across the network, cutting how much data travels for queries that only want a small fraction of each file.

papers.name: FEDORA
papers.gloss: Stores a privacy structure that hides which lookup-table entries are accessed (so an observer cannot tell what the model is searching for) on solid-state drives instead of expensive memory chips; extends drive lifetime 158 times and cuts round-trip delay 24 times for privacy-preserving training.

papers.name: CCZNS
papers.gloss: Brings back hardware compression inside storage drives that require strictly sequential writes (a newer drive format) by having the drive compress data internally while telling the host software where each compressed chunk ends, so the host can manage addresses.

papers.name: OS2G
papers.gloss: A smart network card with its own processors reads training data from cloud object storage and delivers it directly into GPU memory without passing through the main CPU, removing a full extra round-trip.

Measures graph-learning training and finds that loading data from storage is 88 to 91% of total runtime; splitting data into chunks that shuffle independently and reading directly from the solid-state drive into GPU memory without CPU involvement yields 15 times faster training.

papers.name: YOUMU
papers.gloss: Reads model training data straight from a compressed column-format file using random page access, without converting to a different format first; eliminates terabytes of format-conversion disk use and cuts per-node memory footprint by 80%.

papers.name: AnyKey
papers.gloss: Redesigns how a key-value solid-state drive tracks its stored keys so that the tracking information stays bounded in size regardless of how long the keys are; separates the identity of a key from its full content so metadata does not grow with key size.

papers.name: ZRAID
papers.gloss: Stores incomplete parity data (the safety-backup calculations that arise when a sequential-write-only drive has not received a full stripe yet) inside the drive's own write buffer rather than a reserved zone, removing the throughput bottleneck that reserved zones cause.

papers.name: Zebra
papers.gloss: Uses a sequential-write drive's built-in random-write buffer window to absorb incomplete parity updates in a RAID array, matching the repeated-overwrite pattern to the buffer's capability; 1.1 to 4.2 times more throughput.

papers.name: RpcNIC
papers.gloss: A smart network card for remote procedure calls that batches writes across the chip-to-chip bus and keeps serialized data in host memory to avoid slow cross-bus transfers; 2.3 times faster call processing and 2.6 times more throughput over comparable designs.

groups.heading: Memory reliability, system management, and infrastructure
groups.explain: As systems push memory chips harder — more rapid row reads per second, lower voltages, denser storage — physical reliability becomes a concern. Reading one row of a memory chip repeatedly at high speed can flip bits in the rows next to it (a hardware bug called RowHammer). Separately, cloud systems need smarter rules for placing workloads and keeping tenants isolated. These papers study these challenges and propose fixes.

papers.gloss: Tests 160 memory chips and finds that the number of row reads needed to flip a neighboring bit varies by 3.5 times across repeated measurements on the same chip; this undermines the reliability of every existing RowHammer defense, which assumes a fixed safe threshold.

papers.name: ColumnDisturb
papers.gloss: Discovers a new memory chip vulnerability: reading one row can disturb up to 3,072 rows at once through shared column wires — far more than the two rows affected by RowHammer; first measured on 216 memory chips.

papers.name: PuDHammer
papers.gloss: When doing math inside the memory chip, multiple rows are activated at once; this can lower the bit-flip threshold by up to 158 times compared to standard RowHammer on real memory chips; first experimental measurement of this risk.

papers.name: Pegasus
papers.gloss: Maps failing memory addresses to the specific virtual machines whose data lives there, so only at-risk virtual machines are moved rather than the whole server; deployed on over 300,000 production machines, reducing migration cost by over 70%.

papers.name: FleetIO
papers.gloss: Uses multiple learning agents — one per cloud customer — to manage shared solid-state drive resources; agents learn together to balance keeping customers isolated from each other against keeping the hardware well utilized, without hand-tuned rules.

papers.name: Tela
papers.gloss: Picks where to place virtual storage disks in a cloud by modeling how the load on storage servers changes over time, choosing placements that stay balanced not just at creation but across predicted future periods.

papers.name: Virtuoso
papers.gloss: Simulates how an operating system manages virtual memory (handing out pages, invalidating address caches) by imitating observed operating-system decisions rather than running a full operating system; enables fast chip-plus-OS co-design without full-OS simulation cost.

Simplifies the chain of software layers that manage flash memory on tiny microcontrollers (too small for complex storage stacks) by merging separate management steps into coarser unified logic, cutting wasted extra writes without a separate wear-balancing layer.

papers.name: Ariadne
papers.gloss: A compressed swap system for mobile phones that uses small fast-expanding chunks for app data needed at relaunch and large compact chunks for cold data; starts expanding the right chunks before the user even switches back; 50% faster app relaunch.

papers.name: Stramash
papers.gloss: Runs one operating system kernel across two chips with different instruction sets (for example, one Intel-style and one RISC-style) simultaneously, using shared memory as the communication layer instead of passing messages between two separate kernels; 2.1 times faster than a two-kernel approach.

papers.name: Wave
papers.gloss: Moves operating-system housekeeping tasks — scheduling threads, managing memory, handling network calls — from the main CPU to the small processors on a smart network card; frees 16 main CPU cores from memory management with only 1.1 to 7.4% overall slowdown.

papers.name: Concord
papers.gloss: A software-based system for keeping shared data consistent across many server nodes in a short-lived cloud task system; multiple nodes can hold a readable copy simultaneously and are notified to discard it when a write happens; 2.4 times faster and 1.7 times more throughput on a 16-node cluster.

papers.name: InfiniMind
papers.gloss: A memory controller for a brain implant that learns continuously from neural signals on a non-volatile memory chip; four write-reduction methods tailored to the sparse, structured nature of brain signals extend the memory chip's usable lifetime by 23 times.

A model that predicts how fast network processing tasks will run when sharing a smart network card with other tasks; accounts for how they compete for CPU time, data-movement bandwidth, and queue space, enabling accurate service-level agreement management.

papers.name: Gigaflow
papers.gloss: A virtual network switch on a smart network card that caches intermediate processing stages — not just complete flow lookups — so it stays fast even when a cloud customer has a very large set of traffic-routing rules.

papers.name: BTrace
papers.gloss: A redesigned event-recording buffer for smartphones that accepts slightly lower total recording speed in exchange for never dropping events, which is critical for diagnosing crashes and instability on mobile devices.

papers.name: BYOM
papers.gloss: Each application trains its own small model to score which storage jobs are worth sending to fast solid-state drives versus cheap spinning disks; a storage-layer algorithm turns scores into placements using live drive-capacity feedback, without retraining when workloads shift.

papers.name: I-DGNN
papers.gloss: Rewrites a graph-learning network that updates its view of a graph over time as one chain of matrix multiplications, removing repeated full-pipeline passes for each graph update; cuts runtime 65 to 71% over prior dynamic-graph-learning accelerators.

papers.name: MeHyper
papers.gloss: A chip for learning on hypergraph data (where one connection can link more than two nodes at once) that finds shared intermediate values across node-level and connection-level steps and computes each shared value only once; 1,032 times faster than CPU and 10.5 times over GPU.

groups.heading: Restructuring data layouts and how bandwidth is used for specific workloads
groups.explain: Memory chips deliver data in fixed chunks of 64 bytes at a time, but many workloads — graph analytics, genome assembly, math with mostly-zero entries, satellite imaging — only need a few bytes from each chunk. These papers restructure data layouts, computation order, or hardware so most of each fetched chunk is actually used, directly raising how much useful work gets done per byte moved without making the memory chips any faster.

papers.name: NOVA
papers.gloss: A graph-processing chip that separates the 'gather neighbors' and 'send updates' steps so the entire graph stays in memory chips rather than being split and re-read in multiple passes; handles graphs with 2 billion connections; 2.35 times faster than the prior leading chip.

papers.name: Chason
papers.gloss: An FPGA-based chip for multiplying matrices with mostly-zero entries that moves non-zero values across memory channels at runtime to balance how much each channel is used; up to 8 times faster than the prior leading FPGA design and 20 times faster than a high-end gaming GPU.

papers.name: SPARK
papers.gloss: Converts 1.4% of a CPU's fastest on-chip memory into a helper unit for skipping-unimportant-numbers math; skips multiplication when one value is zero; 15 times faster than a standard desktop CPU chip and 152 times better energy efficiency on math that skips many zeros.

papers.name: Buffalo
papers.gloss: Spreads data for high-connection-count graph nodes across non-adjacent memory sections so that graph-learning training on billion-node graphs that do not fit in GPU memory does not cause memory to overflow; 71% faster than standard graph-learning training tools.

papers.name: GSplit
papers.gloss: Assigns graph nodes to GPUs using a pre-computed probability map so each GPU processes a non-overlapping set; no GPU redundantly loads another's data; 4.4 times faster than standard distributed graph-learning training.

papers.name: pulse
papers.gloss: Runs pointer-chasing code — which follows chains of links through data structures — at the memory module where the data lives rather than shipping each link address back to a remote CPU; removes repeated round-trip delays for linked data on rack-scale disaggregated memory.

papers.name: StreamGrid
papers.gloss: Processes three-dimensional point clouds (clouds of measured 3D coordinates from sensors) in a streaming way with a fixed maximum of fast on-chip memory by splitting space into a grid and computing to a defined endpoint before moving on; 10 times faster, 3.9 times better energy, 61% less on-chip memory than prior chips.

papers.name: ARC
papers.gloss: A GPU extension that combines multiple threads' update writes into one before they reach the shared memory's update handler; reduces conflict when many threads update the same location during 3D rendering training.

papers.name: OctoCache
papers.gloss: Restructures 3D map building for autonomous robots: reorders tree traversal so nearby nodes are accessed together, and parallelizes independent map updates; 45 to 88% faster 3D map construction and 3 times faster drone navigation.

papers.name: GPUlog
papers.gloss: Runs a rule-based logic query language (used in program analysis) on a GPU using a new data structure that combines step-by-step index updates with dense array operations that GPUs handle well; 45 times faster than a CPU-based logic query engine.

papers.name: Earth+
papers.gloss: Compresses satellite images on board by comparing each new image against a recent reference from another satellite in the same network and transmitting only the changed pixels; sends 3.3 times less data to ground stations with no quality loss.

papers.name: SEAL
papers.gloss: A chip built directly into an image sensor that encodes each pixel's brightness as a time delay rather than a binary number, then detects keypoints and tracks them inside the sensor before any data leaves the device; 16 to 61 times less delay and 7 times less energy than processing on the host chip.

connect: Every paper in this theme — whether it moves math into memory, fetches data early, compresses numbers, or filters results at the storage drive — is solving the same physical problem: the wires that carry data between chips are slower and costlier per bit than the math units that process it, so the only way to make AI systems faster is to move less data, not do less math.
